correctness.rationale: For identical additive valuations, bilateral envy constraints force \(w_i+p_i=W/n\); balanced transfers force \(p_i=W/n-w_i\). Payment budgets are equivalent to load capacities \(C_i=\lfloor W/n+B_i\rfloor\). Necessity follows by summing all loads and the maximum large-item counts \(\lfloor C_i/r\rfloor\). For sufficiency, assign the k r-valued goods within those count capacities, then all m unit goods using residual integer capacities; both tests guarantee success. The uniform-budget frontier follows from the common capacity threshold. The independent rational exhaustive comparison covered 40,800 parameter profiles and 5,069,616 load vectors; finite tests supplement the universally quantified proof.

value.rationale: The two exact scalar inequalities solve a mathematically natural complete liquidity-feasibility problem for arbitrary heterogeneous household budgets, in a framework where unrestricted indivisible-goods budgeted transfers are computationally difficult. They identify the separate total-funding and large-good fragmentation obstructions, yield a count-only \(O(n)\)-arithmetic construction even with binary multiplicities, and give an exact minimal equal-payment budget. A three-valued boundary example demonstrates why the denominator structure matters. The value is in the precise feasibility region and resource threshold, not a claim of general fair-division decidability.
